https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y4.text: Image source, Volodymyr Zelensky/Telegram Image caption, The Russian agriculture ministry announced it was working to redirect cargo flows to alternative ports following a barrage of Ukrainian drones By Laura Gozzi Published 12 August 2026, 18:20 BST Updated 1 hour ago A "massive" Ukrainian drone and missile strike on Russia's port of Novorossiysk has damaged two major grain export terminals and hit the last big Russian naval base on the Black Sea, reports say. Three people, including an eight-year-old child, were killed and another 24 injured in the overnight attack, local officials said. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had launched rockets, jet and naval drones in a "unique operation" to strike the Russian base, although he did not mention grain terminals being hit. Ukraine's military later said four Russian warships, including two frigates, were hit. Russia's military has not commented publicly commented on the issue. "The occupying fleet and all the infrastructure that supports it will not be safe as long as Russian aggression continues," Zelensky said in a post on social media. Most of Russia's Black Sea fleet is docked in Novorossiysk - one of the largest ports in Russia - after it was forced to vacate its former home base of Sevastopol, in the Russia-occupied Crimean peninsula, which was too exposed to Ukrainian attacks. A major grain trading company confirmed to Russia's TASS news agency that its terminal had been hit, while another told Reuters and Russian outlet RBK the same. The Russian agriculture ministry announced on Wednesday that it was working to redirect cargo flows to ports in the Baltic and Caspian Seas as well as land routes. It did not make any reference to Ukraine's attacks but said it was "taking into account current logistical constraints". Repeated explosions reportedly rang out over Novorossiysk throughout the night as air defences shot down aerial objects. An emergency situation was declared in the city on Wednesday, after the barrage of drones struck areas around the port and damaged pipelines, suspending water supply for the city. Elsewhere in the region a man was killed by drone debris, regional Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said. Several locations in the surrounding Krasnodar region were also struck by "several hundred drones" overnight, Kondratyev added, with dozens of buildings damaged, including homes. For its part, Moscow launched aerial overnight strikes which killed at least 11 civilians in Ukraine between Tuesday and Wednesday. The majority were killed when Russia hit the southern city of Zaporizhzhia with ballistic missiles and glide bombs. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. After a period of relative calm in the Black Sea, over the course of this summer Kyiv and Moscow resumed striking one another's ports and shipping. The last remaining sea route out of Ukraine has been badly affected by several deadly Russian strikes on cargo ships and the port of Odesa, through which Moscow seeks to put off foreign companies from trading with Ukraine. In July, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB) reported a 23% decrease in exports. Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown increasingly adept at carrying out long-range strikes on Russian territory. Its recent attacks on vessels in the eastern Black Sea have disrupted Russia's grain shipments, too. Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter - but according to a Moscow-based analytics company, exports for August could fall by more than half compared to the same month over the last five years due to the disruption in the Black and Azov seas. On Wednesday, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of carrying out strikes on Russian grain and agricultural infrastructure, resulting in a hike in global food prices and growing grain shortages. But Zakharova also said that for its part Russia would continue striking "facilities that [Ukraine's armed forces] use on the Black Sea to destabilise the navigation situation" until "the full elimination of threats to security projected to the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea". Concerns over how the war in Ukraine would affect global food supplies have been persistent since the start of Russia's invasion in 2022. Together, Russia and Ukraine account for a significant share of global grain trade, particularly for buyers in North Africa, the Middle East and parts of Asia. The 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports, did not last after Moscow resumed attacks on vessels using the maritime corridors to Odesa the following year. Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment The National Zoological Garden in Pretoria is incubating the seized eggs and said some of the rescued parrot eggs had successfully hatched. Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment South Africa South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking Rachel Savage in Johannesburg Wed 26 Aug 2026 11.09 EDT First published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking. A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement . View image in fullscreen The seized parrot eggs. Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species. Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment. South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants . The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.” Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added. The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units. South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: 0:50 Russian drone strike hits train near Poland-Ukraine border – video Ukraine Russian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief says Mark Rutte says attack that narrowly missed Boris Johnson and David Petraeus shows Vladimir Putin’s desperation Europe live – latest updates Jennifer Rankin in Brussels and Charlotte Higgins and Amy Hawkins in Kyiv Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.56 EDT First published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The head of Nato has said a Russian drone attack on a train close to Ukraine’s border with Poland would not deter Kyiv’s western backers. Mark Rutte said the strike on a passenger train showed how desperate Vladimir Putin had become. “He thinks that he can stops us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong. Our answer is to increase support,” the Nato general secretary said. European leaders have condemned the strike in which a Russian drone hit a passenger train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday shortly after a convoy of high-level diplomats and former leaders had passed through. The earlier train, which was carrying the former UK prime minister Boris Johnson was running ahead of schedule, may have been the target of the Russian drone strike , Ukrainian Railways has said. A spokesperson forthe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, struck a similar note to Rutte, saying the attack “was a futile attempt by Russia to undermine our support for Ukraine. It will not deter us.” View image in fullscreen Mark Rutte, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, said Ukraine’s western backers would answer the drone strike by increasing support. Photograph: AP The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said the goal of the attacks was “to intimidate Europeans, discourage and above all divide them”. The EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy, Kaja Kallas, said the strike “was clearly a message to the western world”. Speaking on the sidelines of an Arctic conference in Finland, she said: “I think the question for us is what do we take from that message? I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared off, because otherwise, you know, Russia will just achieve what they want, which is the submission of Ukraine.” A spokesperson for Kallas added: “We strongly condemn the latest Russian strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border, including the attack against the passenger train,” and referenced a recent EU decision to approve a €6.1bn tranche of the €90bn loan for Ukraine. “We are acting on the front to equip Ukraine better to defend itself, and we will continue to stand firmly with Ukraine and its right to defend itself against Russian aggression,” the spokesperson said. Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles. View image in fullscreen Kaja Kallas: ‘We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared off.’ Photograph: Petras Malūkas/AFP/Getty Images Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit. The strikes, which prompted air raid warnings in Poland, came as EU diplomats met in Brussels on Monday for last-ditch talks on the rollover of the bloc’s sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian individuals and entities involved in supporting Vladimir Putin’s war. The sanctions are due to expire on Tuesday but their prolongation is being held up by a dispute about whether to remove an individual from the list. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram on Sunday: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries as well as Johnson and the former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike. The diplomatic train, Ukrainian Railways said, had left ahead of schedule and could have been the target of the Russian drone. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to the rail operator. View image in fullscreen Donald Tusk said Poland had been tipped off by its security services and allied intelligence agencies that an attack such as this was likely. Photograph: Piotr Nowak/EPA The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border. “The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”. He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said. https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026/09.text: Menu Search Latest Profile English Contact | About | International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Menu Search International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Latest Profile Fourth International Socialist Equality Party IYSSE About the WSWS Contact Donate Johann Wadephul and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha in Kiev in August 2026 [Photo by Steffen Wurzel / Wikimedia / CC BY 4.0] [Photo by Steffen Wurzel / wikimedia / CC BY 4.0 ] An interview that Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (CDU) gave to the Bild newspaper on September 8 underscores the aggressiveness with which the German government is pushing forward its war course against Russia. With remarkable openness, Wadephul links the military escalation in Ukraine with the profit interests of the German arms industry and the return of Ukrainian refugees of military age to Ukraine. Regarding German military aid for Kiev, Wadephul declares: “We are now the strongest supporter of Ukraine when it comes to financial and military support.” From this he derived the claim of German arms corporations to lucrative contracts: “And naturally it must be the case that the German defence industry profits from this.” During his last visit, he had personally told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that German defence companies “must also be involved” in procurement measures. Nor did Wadephul stop there. He complained that Berlin was “not entirely satisfied” with the volume of Ukrainian orders placed in Germany. The German government had therefore explicitly called on Kiev to “ensure that this improves.” The supposedly selfless “support” for Ukraine is thus described by a representative of the German government for what it is: an instrument of German economic and great-power policy. In the same interview, Wadephul supports the demand by CSU leader Markus Söder to induce Ukrainian men of military age to return to Ukraine. The German government could even help Kiev track them down: “We know who lives here,” Wadephul explains, pointing to data on social benefit recipients, registration status and residence permits. On this basis, the men could be contacted by the Ukrainian government “to tell them that they are to be called up.” Wadephul’s claim that this should take place “without coercion” merely serves to conceal the brutal character of his announcement. The foreign minister advocates making German registration data and information on the residence status of Ukrainian refugees available for their mobilisation by the Ukrainian state. While German arms corporations profit from the war, Ukrainian workers and young people who fled to Germany because of the war are to be sent back to the front as cannon fodder. The class logic of the war emerges openly in these statements. At the top, German arms corporations are to “naturally” profit from the billions spent on war; at the bottom, Ukrainian workers and young people are to pay for it with their lives at the front. The same logic applies in Germany. While Rheinmetall and other arms corporations are showered with ever new major contracts, workers are to finance rearmament through social cuts, higher contributions and falling real wages, while a new generation is mobilised for the Bundeswehr and for a comprehensive war against Russia. The war is not a “defensive war” for “freedom” and “democracy” in the interests of the population, but a class war in the interests of the ruling elites: the profits and geopolitical interests of the corporations and German imperialism are paid for with billions from public coffers and with the lives of workers and young people, and lead inevitably to a Europe-wide catastrophe. Wadephul’s remarks on further escalation against Russia are particularly provocative. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov had described the latest German measures—including the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin—as the “beginning of a real war.” Wadephul brushed aside the warning: “We know very well, and Sergei Lavrov of course also knows, that Russia did this thing in Leipzig.” In fact, to this day the German government has presented no publicly verifiable evidence that Russia was behind the drone incident at Leipzig Airport on August 4. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt merely referred in general terms to investigations and intelligence findings, as well as alleged similarities in components, explosives and ignition technology with earlier operations. Nevertheless, Chancellor Merz declared even before the official “attribution” that Russia was responsible and threatened: “They will pay for this.” The measures announced in response go far beyond diplomatic protest. In addition to closing Russian institutions, Berlin is tightening entry regulations, increasing pressure on Russian ships of the so-called “shadow fleet” and pressing within the EU for further measures against Moscow. It is significant that the German government announced its escalation precisely on September 1—the 87th anniversary of the German invasion of Poland and the beginning of the Second World War. At that time, the Nazis staged the alleged Polish attack on the Gleiwitz radio station in order to present their long-prepared assault as a defensive measure. Now the German government is once again resorting to similar political methods: an unproven accusation is presented as an incontrovertible fact and used to justify long-prepared escalation measures. Berlin is thus creating, step by step, a situation in which any provocation, miscalculation or military confrontation can trigger an open war between NATO and nuclear-armed Russia. This course stands in a dark historical continuity. For the third time in just over a century, German imperialism is directing its strategic offensive eastward and against Russia. In the First World War, the Kaiserreich sought to bring Eastern Europe and large parts of the Russian Empire under its economic and political domination. In the Second World War, the Nazis continued this in the form of a racist war of extermination. On June 22, 1941, more than 3 million German soldiers invaded the Soviet Union. The war aimed at conquering vast territories, controlling raw materials, enslaving and exterminating entire population groups and destroying the Soviet Union. At least 27 million Soviet citizens were killed. Millions of Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. Today, the same fundamental contradictions of the capitalist world system are erupting once again, and with them the great-power ambitions of German imperialism. With the permanent stationing of a tank brigade several thousand strong in Lithuania, German tanks and soldiers are once again in the immediate vicinity of Russia and Belarus. The new German military strategy defines Russia as the main adversary, the Bundeswehr is being built up into the “strongest conventional army in Europe,” and the whole of society is being placed on a war footing within the framework of “comprehensive defence.” Socialism AI by the WSWS SocialismAI.com Questions about this article? Ask Socialism AI What is the historical background of the Historikerstreit and why does the revival of Nolte's arguments matter for understanding German politics today? Can you explain how the 2014 Maidan overthrow in Kiev connected to Germany's shift toward remilitarization at that same time? How did the German and international working class historically organize against militarism before World War I, and what happened to that movement? Ask more questions at SocialismAI.com The fact that Wadephul gave his interview at the same time as the general debate on the federal budget underscores the connection. For 2027, the German government is planning defence spending of almost €152 billion—more than ever before in the history of the Federal Republic. Almost €110 billion is allocated to the regular military budget and nearly €30 billion to the “special fund for the Bundeswehr.” A further €11.6 billion for weapons and equipment for Ukraine is booked outside the defence budget. Defence Minister Boris Pistorius (SPD) explained in his budget speech where the billions are going and what purpose they serve. The war in Ukraine was providing the Bundeswehr with “important lessons,” he declared. It needed modern tanks, artillery, frigates and air defence, as well as thousands of so-called loitering ammunition systems, drones, AI-supported command systems and a “dense network of satellites.” With Uranos AI and the F-35 fighter jets, the “next technological leap” would be made. Uranos AI is explicitly designed to monitor large areas on NATO’s eastern flank and is initially intended to equip the brigade in Lithuania. The major media are taking on the task of ideologically preparing the population for this war course. The current issue of Der Spiegel bears the title: “We Are the Daily Target of Hybrid Warfare—Russia’s Aggression and Germany’s Response.” In his editorial, editor-in-chief Dirk Kurbjuweit openly names the enemy: “Russia is Germany’s enemy.” This is, he writes, a “bitter, infinitely sad sentence,” but it must be spoken “so that everyone can adjust to the situation.” That Kurbjuweit, of all people, is leading this campaign is significant. In February 2014, just a few days after the then German government had proclaimed the end of military restraint at the Munich Security Conference and shortly before the overthrow in Kiev, Der Spiegel published a programmatic article on the revision of German history under the title “The Transformation of the Past.” The issue explicitly raised the question of German guilt for the two world wars. In it, Kurbjuweit gave extensive space to Ernst Nolte, who had relativised National Socialism as a reaction to Bolshevism and thereby triggered the Historikerstreit . Although Kurbjuweit himself admitted that Nolte’s claim of an alleged Jewish “share in the Gulag” had long been an argument used by antisemites, he declared: “But this man was not wrong about everything.” Kurbjuweit quoted the Berlin historian and Nolte supporter Jörg Baberowski with the notorious words: “Hitler was not a psychopath, he was not vicious.” At the time, the Socialist Equality Party warned that the return of German militarism was inseparably bound up with the whitewashing of the historical crimes of German imperialism. Twelve years later, the significance of this warning is becoming ever clearer. Germany is rearming to become the strongest military power in Europe, stationing German combat units in the East once again, producing weapons for attacks deep into Russian territory, mobilising young people for the army, openly declaring Russia the enemy, and arming and financing a regime in Kiev that celebrates Ukrainian Nazi collaborators such as Stepan Bandera as national heroes. The revival of fascism and the escalation of war cannot be stopped by appeals to Merz, Wadephul, Pistorius or other capitalist forces, all of whom support the course of rearmament and the shift to the right in one form or another. They can be halted only through an independent movement of the German, Russian, Ukrainian and international working class against war and its cause, the capitalist profit system. The Sozialistische Gleichheitspartei (Socialist Equality Party) is fighting for this perspective in the Berlin state election on September 20. Under the slogans “Two World Wars Are Enough!” and “Socialism, Not War!” it opposes the war coalition of the established parties and fights to build an international socialist movement of the working class against militarism, fascism and war. https://www.dw.com/en/uk-iran-highly-lik.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OBXx PM Andy Burnham said it would 'almost certainly' be Iran's IRGC that was pulling the strings Image: House of Commons/PA Images/picture alliance Advertisement The British government has accused Iran of involvement in a security alert outside a UK/US airbase in southern England last month , summoning the ambassador and announcing sanctions against two individuals. Five British nationals were arrested in the vicinity of the RAF Fairford airbase on September 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses. They were later released on bail under strict conditions , and another arrest followed days later . Police had already said they were considering the possibility of a foreign state actor's involvement, not least given RAF Fairford's importance to the US Air Force as one of the European bases that handles heavy bombers like B-1's and B-52's, with ample range to reach Iran . Some of the more advanced US bombers at RAF Fairford were ordered home after the incident [FILE: September 29, 2026] Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS What did Prime Minister Andy Burnham tell parliament? Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in the House of Commons on Monday that the UK might yet put further sanctions on Iran in response. He said there were indications of Iran coordinating the potential plot. "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," he said. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil." The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited. Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the vans. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said. Burnham told the Commons that Iran could potentially face further sanctions Image: House of Commons/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance Foreign Secretary Miliband says Iranian ambassador summoned Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil." Iran's state news agency IRNA reported Ambassador Ali Moussavi as "categorically rejecting the accusations" and calling on the British government "to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any." Miliband said that two individuals would be subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification. He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network. Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas." How viable or dangerous the attack plot really was remains something of an open question, what's certain is that the young men were able to cause a major disturbance and an international incident [FILE: September 27, 2026] Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance Joint statement from 29 countries condemns 'Iran's use of violent attacks' Shortly afterwards, a total of 29 countries issued a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks." It said these included "the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners." All of the so-called "Five Eyes" alliance and most European NATO members were listed among the signatories, including but not limited to the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Spain and Ireland. In the aftermath of the September 27 incident at Fairford, the high-tech US B-1 bombers left the airbase . The older and larger contingent of B-52's remained there. RAF Fairford is one of several airbases in southern England with a large US usage footprint. It's located around two hours' drive west of London, in a rural area north of Swindon. As with most such bases, it can trace its roots back to the second World War when Nazi Germany occupied most of mainland Europe and Allied powers were operating air raids and preparing for the D-Day landings out of Britain. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/live.text: The defence is to begin presenting its case in Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court, where he faces allegations of rape and sexual assault against six women. The prosecution’s case has drawn to a close after nearly two weeks of evidence, with the jury to hear from the defence today. In yesterday’s hearing, the jury was told by the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, that the indecent assault charge against Brand has been amended to attempted indecent assault. It relates to an allegation that Brand grabbed a female MTV worker by the arm and tried to drag her into a toilet. Bennathan told jurors he had reached the conclusion that there was insufficient evidence to support the charge of indecent assault. The court also heard Brand was interviewed by police on four occasions – in November and December 2023, January 2024 and July 2025.
